sources.title: All About Venus - NASA Space Place

researchNotes.title: A bright neighbor
researchNotes.text: Venus is the second planet from the Sun and one of Earth's closest planetary neighbors. From Earth it can look like a brilliant point of light near sunrise or sunset, brighter than any other planet in our sky. This gives a strong age-five opening: Venus looks gentle and shiny from far away, but it is a very different world up close.

researchNotes.title: Earth's almost-twin size, not twin weather
researchNotes.text: Venus is often called Earth's twin or sister planet because it is rocky and only a little smaller than Earth. That comparison is useful for young readers if it is kept simple: Venus and Earth are nearly the same size, but Venus does not feel like home. Its air, heat, clouds, and surface conditions are extremely different.

researchNotes.title: The hottest planet
researchNotes.text: Venus is the hottest planet in the solar system, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun. NASA gives a surface temperature of about 872 degrees Fahrenheit, or 467 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead. For age five, the safe comparison is that Venus is much too hot for people, animals, or puddles of water on the ground.

researchNotes.title: A thick blanket of air
researchNotes.text: Venus has a very thick atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide, with clouds of sulfuric acid. That thick air traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect. NASA also describes the pressure on the surface as about 93 times Earth's sea-level pressure, like being deep underwater on Earth. For young children, this can become a concrete idea: Venus has air that presses and traps heat like an enormous heavy blanket.

researchNotes.title: Clouds hide the ground
researchNotes.text: Venus looks smooth and cloudy in visible-light spacecraft images because a global cloud layer hides its rocky surface. Scientists learned to map the hidden ground with radar, especially from NASA's Magellan spacecraft. This supports a strong picture-book turn: first readers see the soft clouds, then the book 'peeks underneath' with radar images.

researchNotes.title: Rocky land with volcanoes and craters
researchNotes.text: Venus is a terrestrial, rocky planet. Radar maps and spacecraft studies show broad plains, mountains, volcanoes, lava features, and impact craters. Magellan data showed evidence of volcanism and mapped nearly the whole surface. The book can use this without implying a child could stand there: Venus has real rocky land, but it is hidden below dangerous hot clouds.

researchNotes.title: A day longer than a year
researchNotes.text: Venus rotates very slowly. A Venus day, measured by one spin against the stars, lasts about 243 Earth days, while a Venus year around the Sun lasts about 225 Earth days. NASA Space Place phrases this clearly for children: a day on Venus is a little longer than a year on Venus. This is a memorable throughline, but the exact numbers should stay as optional extras rather than overload the main text.

researchNotes.title: Backward sunrise
researchNotes.text: Venus spins in the opposite direction from Earth and most other planets. Because of that backward rotation, if someone could safely watch from Venus, the Sun would rise in the west and set in the east. This fact is surprising and child-friendly, but it should be framed as a thought experiment because the real surface is not safe for people.

researchNotes.title: No moons, no rings
researchNotes.text: Venus has no moons and no rings. This is simple enough for the main text or a small fact bubble. It also helps contrast Venus with familiar picture-book images of other planets, especially Saturn's rings or Earth's Moon.

researchNotes.title: Robots went first
researchNotes.text: Many spacecraft have been sent to Venus. NASA's Mariner 2 was the first successful mission to another planet when it flew past Venus in 1962. Mariner 10 photographed the cloud-covered planet, Pioneer Venus studied it from orbit, and Magellan used radar to map the surface. This supports a gentle explorer arc: people learn about Venus by sending robot helpers.

researchNotes.title: Careful age framing
researchNotes.text: Venus's heat, crushing pressure, sulfuric-acid clouds, and toxic atmosphere are scientifically important, but for age five they should be described without horror. Avoid suggesting a child travels onto the surface. Better approaches include 'robot explorers,' 'too hot for puddles,' 'clouds hiding a rocky world,' and 'look from far away.' Do not claim there is life on Venus; sources discuss scientific questions about clouds, but that is too speculative for the central narrative here.

handoffNotes: Promising throughline: Venus is a shining neighbor that looks soft from far away, then reveals surprises under its clouds. The approved image set intentionally mixes real-color/cloud spacecraft views, radar surface globes, one radar landscape, and one NASA child-facing illustration. Keep numbers sparse in main text for age 5; use extras for 225/243 days if needed. Avoid generated images unless the author needs a specific child-facing robot-explorer moment not covered by the NASA pool.
